variants.name: Paging 3 PagingSource with keyset keys
variants.implementation_notes: androidx.paging provides the structure: implement PagingSource<Key, Value> and have load() return LoadResult.Page(data, prevKey, nextKey) where the keys are the keyset ids at the edges of the page (afterId/beforeId) rather than page numbers, then expose Pager(PagingConfig(pageSize = 20)) { pagingSourceFactory }.flow as Flow<PagingData<Item>>; null keys mark the edges, so end-of-collection is structural instead of a token string on the wire. This is the default on Android/Compose; a plain coroutine flow loop is the alternative off-platform.
pitfalls: Keys must be stable and serializable because Paging 3 persists them for refresh and drop handling: a cursor encoding a mutable sort value makes refresh jump, and getRefreshKey must map the anchor item id back to a load key deliberately.
Data changes are signalled with LoadResult.Invalid, not with an exception: throwing inside load fails the whole generation instead of triggering a reload.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Flow loop over nextPageToken
variants.idiom_name: cold flow { } that chains pages, emitAll(page.items.asFlow())
variants.implementation_notes: Off Android (or without the Paging dependency) the idiom is a cold Flow whose builder loops until the token is null, emitting each page's items with emitAll(items.asFlow()); operators such as buffer, flowOn and cancellation propagate through the chain, which makes the sequential cursor protocol ordinary coroutine code. Prefer PagingSource when the consumer is a Compose list that needs placeholders and refresh semantics; prefer the Flow loop for services, CLIs and KMP code.
pitfalls: Cancelling the collector stops the flow mid-page, so never persist the cursor outside the flow unless the consumer can resume deliberately; a resumed cursor belongs to the collector, not to the flow instance.
Emitting a whole page as one value makes memory proportional to the page and defeats backpressure - emit elements (emitAll(items.asFlow())) or apply buffer() knowingly.
